title: seunshare 3.10 Let Unprivileged Users Delete Root Files and Kill Root Processes
summary: The SUSE Security Team audited seunshare — the setuid-root utility SELinux uses to isolate untrusted programs — and found two local denial-of-service bugs in version 3.10. One missing flag enables a symlink race that routes arbitrary root file deletion through the sandbox tool itself. The other lets any unprivileged user kill root-owned processes by supplying a context string. Both are fixed in 3.11.
body:
`seunshare` runs setuid-root. It sets up mount namespaces to confine untrusted programs. It is, in principle, the thing standing between an untrusted user and the rest of the system.

It had two local denial-of-service bugs in version 3.10.

The SUSE Security Team published their findings on July 15, 2026. The research is their own — named functions, commit references, reproduction steps. Not vendor marketing. Read the original.

## The rm_rf symlink race

`rm_rf()` cleans up temporary directories after use. It calls `fstatat()` to check whether a directory entry is a subdirectory, then calls `openat()` to open it. Between the check and the open, an unprivileged user can swap the directory entry for a symlink pointing to an arbitrary location. `openat()` without `O_NOFOLLOW` follows it. `O_DIRECTORY` sounds like it would catch this; it does not — the flag still follows symlinks that point to directories.

Result: an unprivileged local user in the unconfined SELinux domain can arrange for seunshare to recursively delete root-owned files anywhere on the filesystem.

Fixed in 3.11 by adding `O_NOFOLLOW` to the `openat()` call. Upstream commit `38f0a4d9a`.

## The --kill context switch

`seunshare` has a `--kill` switch combined with `-Z context`. The `killall()` function sends SIGKILL to all processes matching a user-supplied SELinux context string. An unconfined user supplies the unconfined context string and root-owned processes running in the unconfined domain receive SIGKILL.

Fixed in 3.11 by removing `--kill` and the entire `killall()` function. Upstream commit `572db2fa`. When the only correct fix is deletion, that is what gets deleted.

## The domain transition that is not there

On Fedora and openSUSE with targeted policy, there is no domain transition defined from `unconfined_t` to `seunshare_t`. An unconfined user invokes seunshare and remains in the unconfined domain throughout. SELinux enforcing mode is active. It does not help.

This is not a flaw in the two bugs. It is a policy gap that elevates their practical impact to something closer to root-equivalent even on a hardened system.

## CVE status

None. The upstream SELinux userspace project does not actively assign CVEs. SUSE offered to handle assignment and was awaiting clarification from Red Hat developers upstream to avoid duplicate IDs. The fixes landed in 3.11 before that resolved.

Fedora 44 backported the patches. openSUSE Tumbleweed running policycoreutils 3.10 was vulnerable at publication time.

## Other findings

The audit flagged additional design concerns: untrusted data copied back via rsync could deposit dangerous files in user directories; complex UID-flipping logic maintained unusual privilege states; the privileged parent process lacked environment variable sanitization; and `umask()` behavior could create world-readable or world-writable files.

`seunshare` is a program for running untrusted things safely. The audit found the program was not entirely safe to run.
